universal.heading: How to Use This Roadmap

groups.heading: Universal 20-Layer Research Protocol
items: Begin with scope: write what the theme includes and what it does not include.
Build the vocabulary first: 12-25 precise terms, definitions, distinctions and commonly confused concepts.
Trace origin and evolution: who introduced important terms or theories, when, in which work/document, and how meaning changed.
Build a timeline only of turning points that explain the present debate; do not collect chronology for its own sake.
Identify analytical frameworks or theories that explain causes, mechanisms and outcomes.
Divide the theme into political, economic, social, institutional, technological, legal/ethical, environmental, security, Pakistan-specific and global/comparative dimensions where relevant.
Prepare a causal map: underlying drivers → mechanisms → immediate effects → long-term effects → feedback loops.
Create an institution/stakeholder map: who makes policy, implements it, finances it, is affected by it, and can block or enable reform.
Collect recent evidence only after the analytical framework is clear. Every number must have indicator, value, place, year and source.
Build both Pakistan and global columns; use the same indicator when making comparisons.
Collect case studies: Pakistan, a strong international case, a developing-country comparator and a cautionary/failure case.
Collect relevant laws, constitutional provisions, policies, treaties, strategies, judgments and official guidance; verify current status.
Build a report/index bank, but read methodology before using rankings.
Prepare only a small bank of verified quotations; trace wording to a primary work, official transcript or scholarly edition.
Prepare serious counterarguments and trade-offs.
Distinguish problems from symptoms and solutions from slogans.
Prepare future scenarios: baseline, reform, disruption and technology/geopolitical/climate scenario where relevant.
Build cross-theme links so evidence can be reused intelligently.
Convert research into website blocks: Overview, Concepts, Timeline, Dimensions, Data, Pakistan, Global Cases, Debates, Laws/Policies, Solutions, Essay Angles and Sources.
Before publication, re-check date, definition, source, quotation wording, legal status and whether a newer official edition exists.

groups.heading: Evidence Capture Card — Use for Every Statistic
Source & Verification Rules
items: Primary/official sources first: laws, budgets, regulators, statistics offices, court documents, treaties, official databases and institutional reports.
Major multilateral/academic sources second: UN agencies, World Bank, IMF, ILO, UNESCO, FAO, WMO, IPCC, IEA, IRENA, SIPRI, WIPO and established universities/research institutes.
News sources are for developments, examples and statements; they should not replace primary structural data when primary data exists.
Never save a screenshot or number without source title, publication year and preferably page/table or dataset link.
If reputable sources disagree, record definitions and measurement periods before choosing one.
For politically contested topics, separate facts, legal findings, official positions, scholarly interpretation and opinion.

universal.intro: This document gives research directions rather than ready-made notes. Each theme identifies what must be defined, traced, compared, measured, verified, debated or converted into a website content block. Universal research rules, question matrices, scenario tests, search procedures, publishing architecture and quality-control checks are stated once at the beginning and apply to every theme. The theme files therefore concentrate on unique concepts, evidence needs, Pakistan-specific directions, comparative cases, debates, reforms and essay angles.

universal.heading: Universal Operating Modules — Apply Once to Every Theme

groups.heading: Universal Analytical Question Matrix
items: For every dimension, establish five things: current position → main drivers → affected groups → strongest measurable evidence → principal policy trade-offs.
Test commonly repeated claims before using them; flag assertions that are influential but weakly evidenced.
Separate causes, mechanisms and outcomes; do not treat correlation as causation.
Compare what changed during the last decade with structural features that remained persistent.
Disaggregate national averages by region, sector, gender, income, age or other relevant groups whenever data allows.
Choose international comparisons only when the comparator is genuinely relevant to Pakistan; record why it is comparable and where the comparison breaks down.
Define measurable indicators of success before proposing reforms.

groups.heading: Universal Future-Scenario Grid
items: Baseline — project what follows if present trends and existing policy continue.
Reform — identify what changes if the strongest feasible reforms are implemented.
Stress — identify a plausible shock that could materially worsen the problem.
Technology — test how new technology could alter the problem, the available solutions or the distribution of gains and losses.
Institutional — identify which outcomes depend most on implementation capacity, political incentives, coordination or public trust.
Equity — identify who may lose from an otherwise beneficial reform and what mitigation would be required.

groups.heading: Universal Cross-Theme Reuse Map
items: Governance and institutional capacity — identify which institutions determine implementation and outcomes.
Economy and inequality — trace who pays, who gains, and what productivity, employment or fiscal effects follow.
Technology — examine what changes through digitization, artificial intelligence, data, infrastructure or innovation.
Human development — connect the theme with education, health, gender, youth, skills and social mobility where relevant.
Climate and resources — connect exposure, resilience, energy, water, food or ecological constraints where relevant.
World order and security — connect trade, diplomacy, conflict, sanctions, strategic competition, international institutions or international law where relevant.

groups.heading: Universal Search & Collection Sequence
items: Begin with an official-source search using the exact theme plus its core indicator, policy or institution.
Open the latest primary report first and search inside it for the exact indicator or term instead of reading randomly.
For global comparison, use the same indicator in a multilateral database so definitions and measurement periods remain comparable.
For case studies, search policy name + evaluation + outcome + institution/university; prefer evaluated results over publicity material.
For laws and policies, verify whether the instrument is enacted, draft, amended, suspended, expired, repealed or superseded.
For quotations, locate the original book, paper, judgment, report or speech; do not rely on quotation websites.
Record every useful source immediately with title, institution/author, year, page/table or dataset link, and access date.

groups.heading: Universal Website Content Architecture
items: Theme Overview — scope, significance and central debate.
Key Concepts — glossary cards for essential terms and distinctions.
Origin & Timeline — only milestones that explain the present debate.
Dimensions — separate evidence blocks for major analytical dimensions.
Data Dashboard — verified indicators with definition, year and source.
Pakistan Lens — diagnosis, institutions, policy status, implementation record and local evidence.
Global Comparisons — carefully chosen cases with lessons, enabling conditions and limits.
Laws / Policies / Reports — linked primary-source library.
Debates & Counterarguments — strongest evidence-based case on competing sides.
Solutions — short-, medium- and long-term reforms with responsible institutions and implementation barriers.
Essay Angles — thesis questions, outline directions and cross-theme links.
Sources — full citation details plus the last verification/update date.

groups.heading: Universal Research Pitfalls
items: Do not build an entire diagnosis around one headline ranking or dramatic statistic.
Do not mix years, units, definitions or measurement methods in the same comparison.
Do not treat a successful foreign model as automatically transferable; record enabling conditions and contextual limits.
Do not use quotations without primary verification.
Do not confuse a policy announcement with implementation, coverage or outcome.
Do not list reforms without identifying obstacles, trade-offs, sequencing and responsible institutions.
Do not publish fast-changing statistics without a visible last-updated date.

groups.heading: Universal Completion Checklist
items: Core vocabulary is precise and commonly confused concepts are distinguished.
Historical evolution is reduced to meaningful turning points rather than chronology for its own sake.
At least three analytical frameworks are available to explain the theme.
Every major dimension has evidence, and the argument supported by each statistic is clear.
Pakistan-specific data, institutions, policy status and implementation questions are covered.
The case bank contains strong international comparisons, a developing-country comparator where useful, and at least one cautionary or failure case.
Primary legal and policy documents have been located and their current status verified.
Serious counterarguments are addressed with evidence rather than slogans.
Solutions are sequenced and connected to institutions, resources, incentives and implementation barriers.
Fast-changing statistics, quotations and legal claims carry a source and verification date.
The research file can be converted directly into website blocks without further structural research.
